extracted.intended_audience: theologians, seminarians, students and scholars of dogmatic theology
extracted.subtask_description: Scholastic and patristic exposition and argumentation about divine grace, perseverance, predestination, and related notions (merit, faith, petition/prayer), citing councils, Church Fathers, and scholastic authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prayer as means to receive perseverance (donum perseverantiae)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perseverance is properly asked of God in prayer; when saints pray the Lord taught the Lord's Prayer so that what is essentially asked is perseverance — prayer is the ordinary way God grants perseverance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple Augustine citations (De Dono Perseverantiae) and Suarez emphasize that the Church should not rely on disputation but on daily prayers: 'Orat ut credentes perseverent; Deus ergo donat perseverantiam usque in finem.' Also: one who thinks he has perseverance from himself does not pray for it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverantia must be persistent in prayer and life
rubrics_metrics.description: Prayer for perseverance is required not once but continuously — it must endure for the whole life and be repeated in occasions of temptation to preserve commands and overcome trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly stated: perseverance in prayer 'requisita est, ut non semel tantum aut iterum fiat, set ut toto tempore vitae duret, et praesertim ut in occurrentibus occasionibus ... repetatur.' See Suarez and Palmieri for further details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infallibilitas of fruit depends on petition (impetration) not on merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Infallibility (certainty of receiving a divine fruit) does not belong to merit in the sense of congruous reward but to the act of impetration (prayer); thus petition rather than meritorious congruity grounds certain divine promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suarez: 'Infallibilitas non convenit merito ... sed ratione impetrationis quae propriae soli orationi ... respondet.' Therefore petition for perseverance should accompany merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donum perseverantiae distinct from confirmatio in gratia
rubrics_metrics.description: The gift of perseverance (donum perseverantiae) must not be confused with confirmation in grace (confirmatio in gratia); they are distinct theological notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are referred to Schiffini, Palmieri, and Gutberlet for nuanced theological argumentation distinguishing these concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratia not given according to human merits (gratiam non secundum merita dari)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Church and patristic tradition reject that divine grace is distributed according to our merits; grace is gratuitous and not merited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited as emphasized since the fourth century and formally defined by the Council of Trent (Sess. VI). Numerous patristic and scholastic citations (Augustine, Tridentine canons) support this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merit and reward relation (meritum et merces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merit and reward are related such that 'merces' is that recompensed to someone for their work; rewarding for work is an act of justice — but this must be reconciled with grace being gratuitous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Thomas cited (Summa Theol., 1a 2ae, qu. 114, art. 1). Discussion distinguishes how merit relates to gratuity and to the divine gift of grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritum de condigno / de congruo distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology around merit (meritum de condigno vs. meritum de congruo) matters: some theologians prefer 'meritum digni'; distinctions affect how one talks about retribution and congruity with grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note on usage (Eck, others) and references to canonical and scholastic debates; see Taparelli and related citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace as beginning/foundation/root of justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace is the 'initium, fundamentum et radix omnis iustificationis' — the cause and starting point of justification, preceding any merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations to Conc. Trident., Sess. VI and Thomistic sources stressing that justification is by grace, not by human works alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faith necessary for justification and salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: Without faith it is impossible to please God; no one is justified or saved without faith, properly understood in relation to divine revelation and grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciliar and scriptural citations (Rom., Hebrews, Thomistic commentary) affirm faith's necessity for justification (e.g., Sess. III, cap. 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: God wills all to be saved while preserving free will
rubrics_metrics.description: God desires the salvation of all and wills man to be able to be saved, yet this does not remove or override free will — God's will for all to be saved coexists with human freedom and divine justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural proofs and patristic citations cited (e.g., 1 Tim. II, Rom. passages) and theological works (Pohle-Preuss, Ruiz) explore compatibility with free will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between efficacious and sufficient grace and their distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a doctrinal distinction between efficacious grace and sufficient grace; the distribution and operation of these graces (who receives efficacious grace, who receives sufficient grace) is theologically significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to Tridentine and scholastic discussions; statement that God gave efficacious grace to many and did not remove sufficient grace from anyone (cited passages, theological commentary). See supra discussion on 'gratia efficax' and 'sufficiens'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predestination defined as preparation of grace and gift of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Predestination (praedestinatio) is the preparation of grace (and future glory); predestination precedes and is not grounded in foreseen human merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes: 'Praedestinatio est gratiae praeparatio, gratia vero iam ipsa donatio.' Tridentine sensibility presupposes predestination as dogma; numerous scholastic citations (Summa, De Dono Perseverantiae) elaborate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predestination not based on foreseen merits
rubrics_metrics.description: Election/predestination is not to be explained as based on foreseen natural merits; to suppose predestination is due to foreseen merits is to invert the gratuitous character of grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations to Thomistic arguments and defenses against views that tie predestination to human merits; references to controversies (Bañez, Suarez, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and identity of the predestined known only to God
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise number of the predestined and who they are belong solely to God's knowledge; human speculation about the exact number is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: St. Thomas and other scholastic authorities cited: 'soli Deo est cognitus numerus electorum.' Various speculative counts by medieval divines are mentioned but rejected as certain knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: God does not command the impossible; he admonishes to do what you can and pray for what you cannot
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine precepts do not oblige to impossibilities: 'Deus impossibilia non iubet, sed iubendo admonet, et facere quod possis et petere quod non possis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This maxim is cited (De Natura et Gratia) and used to explain moral responsibility in connection with grace and human ability; see also Tridentine canons on impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural and patristic authority central to theological proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal claims are supported and justified by extensive citation of Scripture, Church Fathers, and Councils; patristic quotations serve as primary evidence for dogmatic positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous quotations (Augustine, Chrysostom, Councils like Trent, scriptural passages) used throughout to ground arguments about grace and predestination.

rubrics_metrics.name: The compatibility question of divine foreknowledge and free will
rubrics_metrics.description: The text treats the problem of how infallible divine foreknowledge and predestination are compatible with human free will; theological authorities offer defenses and explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to Franzelin, Pohle-Preuss, and other theologians who address this compatibility; counsel to consult specific works for fuller treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical pastoral implication: never despair over any person in this life
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite doctrines on predestination and the hardness of some hearts, one must not despair about any person in this life — there's always hope for conversion while life remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited Augustine's Retractationes and other patristic consolations; pastoral tone advising hope and ongoing prayer for souls.
